question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Despite the professor's best efforts to explain the complex theory, it took me a while to decipher the meaning of the text.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. interpret.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "decipher" means to succeed in understanding, interpreting, or making out the meaning of something that is obscure, unclear, or written in code. (किसी अस्पष्ट बात का अर्थ समझना / गूढ़ार्थ निकालना)
◦ Example: It took the historian years to decipher the ancient manuscript.

• In the given sentence, "it took me a while to decipher the meaning of the text" means it took time to interpret / work out the meaning, so "interpret" is the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "predict" (भविष्यवाणी करना): to say that something will happen in the future; it does not mean to understand something already written.

• Option 3: "conceal" (छिपाना): to hide something from view or keep it secret — this is the opposite of what "decipher" means.

• Option 4: "foresee" (पूर्वानुमान लगाना): to know or realise something will happen before it does; unrelated to understanding a difficult text.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "decipher": decode, unravel, interpret, construe, make out.

• Do not confuse "decipher" with "describe" or "discover", which are often used as distractors in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The doctor knew that Ravindra would recover from dengue soon and do the kind of work he was doing before.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. had been doing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The reporting verb of the sentence is "knew", which is in the Simple Past Tense. When the main clause of a sentence is in the past tense, the tense in the subordinate clause must also be shifted backward according to the Rule of Sequence of Tenses.

• The subordinate clause describes an action, "the kind of work he ___ before", which was going on continuously before the point of time referred to by "knew" and had not yet finished at that point — this is the exact situation described by the Past Perfect Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Past Perfect Continuous Tense: Subject + had been + V1 + ing (+ Object), used for an action that started before a certain point in the past and continued up to (or near) that point.

• Applying the rule: "he was doing" (past continuous) must become "he had been doing" to correctly show that the work had been going on continuously before the time referred to by "knew".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "would do" is incorrect — this is the simple future-in-the-past form, used for a future action, not a continuous action that was happening before a past point.

• Option 2: "had been done" is incorrect — this is a passive construction (had been + V3), but the subject "he" is the doer of the work here, so the active form is needed.

• Option 3: "would have been doing" is incorrect — this form (would have been + V1-ing) expresses an unfulfilled continuous action in the past conditional sense, which does not fit the plain narration required here.

NOTE

• Key marker words that usually signal the Past Perfect Continuous Tense: "before", "till/until then", "since", "for" (with a past time reference).

• Do not confuse Past Perfect Continuous (had been + V-ing) with Past Perfect Simple (had + V3); the continuous form is used specifically to stress the duration of the action.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options.
The English / often / fought / French.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. French.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct sentence should read: "The English often fought the French."

• Rule — Definite Article "the" with Nationalities: The definite article "the" is used before an adjective of nationality (such as English, French, Dutch, Spanish) when it is used as a collective plural noun referring to the entire people/nation of that country.

• In the given sentence, "French" (referring to the French people as a nation) is missing the required article "the" before it; it should be "the French", exactly as "The English" correctly has "the" before it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "often" is correct as written — it is an adverb of frequency, correctly placed between the subject and the main verb.

• Option 3: "fought" is correct as written — it is the correct Past Tense (V2) form of the irregular verb "fight".

• Option 4: "The English" is correct as written — "the" is correctly used before the nationality adjective "English" used as a collective noun for the English people.

NOTE

• Other nationality words that take "the" when used as a collective plural noun: the French, the Dutch, the Chinese, the Japanese, the Spanish, the Swiss.

• However, when the same word is used as an adjective before a noun (e.g. "French cuisine", "English literature") or refers to the language, no article is used.

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in active voice.
Why is the rotten apple being eaten by you?
option_1: Why were you eating the rotten apple?
option_2: Why you are eating the rotten apple?
option_3: Why have you eaten the rotten apple?
option_4: Why are you eating the rotten apple?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Why are you eating the rotten apple?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Why is the rotten apple being eaten by you?" is in the Passive Voice, Present Continuous Tense, framed as a question ("Why" + is + Subject + being + V3 + by + Agent).

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense (Passive to Active, Wh-question):
◦ Passive: Wh-word + is/am/are + Object + being + V3 + by + Subject?
◦ Active: Wh-word + is/am/are + Subject + V1+ing + Object?

• Applying the rule: the agent "you" becomes the subject; the object "the rotten apple" becomes the object of the active sentence; "is being eaten" becomes "are eating" (as the new subject "you" takes "are").
◦ Active: Why are you eating the rotten apple?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Why were you eating the rotten apple?" is incorrect — "were...eating" is Past Continuous Tense, not Present Continuous.

• Option 2: "Why you are eating the rotten apple?" is incorrect — the word order is wrong for a question; the auxiliary "are" must come before the subject "you" in an interrogative sentence.

• Option 3: "Why have you eaten the rotten apple?" is incorrect — "have eaten" is Present Perfect Tense, which changes the meaning and tense of the original sentence.

NOTE

• In Wh-questions, the auxiliary verb always comes immediately after the question word and before the subject: Wh-word + auxiliary + subject + main verb.

• Common tense-mixing errors like this (changing Present Continuous to Past/Perfect) are a favourite SSC distractor pattern in voice-change questions.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. dictators may rise to power and inaugurate
B. a new regime with dramatic suddenness
C. and success under suitable conditions
D. democracy is always a slow growth
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. DABC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Reading the parts in the order D-A-B-C gives a grammatically complete and logically coherent sentence: "Democracy is always a slow growth [D]; dictators may rise to power and inaugurate [A] a new regime with dramatic suddenness [B] and success under suitable conditions [C]."

• Rule for sentence-rearrangement (Para jumbles): Look for the part containing the main/independent subject-verb combination to start the sentence, and then trace the logical/grammatical continuity — a linking word or a continuing verb phrase — through the remaining parts.

• Here, part D ("democracy is always a slow growth") introduces the main subject "democracy" and sets up a contrast, part A introduces the contrasting subject "dictators" with the verb phrase "may rise to power and inaugurate", which grammatically demands an object — supplied by B ("a new regime..."), which in turn is completed by C ("...and success under suitable conditions").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "DCAB" is incorrect — placing C ("and success under suitable conditions") right after D breaks the logical link between "inaugurate" (in A) and its object "a new regime" (in B).

• Option 2: "ACBD" is incorrect — starting with A ("dictators may rise...") without the contrasting idea in D first makes the sentence lack a clear starting context.

• Option 4: "ABCD" is incorrect — placing D ("democracy is always a slow growth") at the end breaks the natural contrast structure that should open the sentence.

NOTE

• In such contrast-based jumbled sentences, the part that sets up the general/contrasting idea (often signalled by words like "always", "generally") usually comes first, followed by the specific/contrasting example.

• Always read the fully reconstructed sentence once at the end to check it makes complete logical and grammatical sense before finalising the order.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.
Happiness is not something you ________ (adjourn) for the future. It is something you design for the present.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. postpone.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "adjourn" means to put off or delay something to a later time. (स्थगित करना / टालना)
◦ Example: The meeting was adjourned till next Monday due to lack of quorum.

• Its closest synonym among the given options is "postpone", which also means to delay an event or action to a later time, matching the meaning required by the sentence: "Happiness is not something you postpone (adjourn) for the future."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "decimate" (नष्ट करना): to kill, destroy, or drastically reduce something in number — unrelated to delaying.

• Option 2: "rejuvenate" (पुनर्जीवित करना): to make someone or something look or feel young, fresh, or energetic again.

• Option 3: "constitute" (गठन करना): to be a part of a whole, or to legally establish something — unrelated to delaying.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "adjourn": defer, postpone, put off, delay, suspend, prorogue (used specifically for adjourning a legislative session).

• Do not confuse "adjourn" with "adjust" (to alter slightly to fit) — a common SSC distractor pair.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The fields are full of crops existing in large quantities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. that are abundant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase "existing in large quantities" means the same as the word "abundant", which means existing or available in large quantities; plentiful. (प्रचुर मात्रा में उपलब्ध)
◦ Example: The region has an abundant supply of fresh water.

• Replacing the underlined phrase with the single word "abundant" (in the structure "that are abundant") preserves the exact meaning of the original sentence: "The fields are full of crops that are abundant."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "that are sufficient" (पर्याप्त): means "enough for a purpose", which is not the same as "existing in large quantities" — sufficient does not necessarily mean plentiful.

• Option 2: "that are limited" (सीमित): means restricted in quantity — this is nearly the opposite of "existing in large quantities".

• Option 3: "that are customized" (अनुकूलित): means specially made or adapted to particular requirements — unrelated to quantity.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "abundant": plentiful, ample, copious, profuse, bountiful.

• Its antonym is "scarce" / "scanty", meaning insufficient or limited in supply — a common antonym pairing tested by SSC.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Fullfil.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "Fulfil" (British spelling, single "l" after "fu" and single "l" at the end) or "Fulfill" (American spelling, with double "ll" at the end only) — meaning to carry out or achieve something, such as a promise, duty, or ambition.

• The given option "Fullfil" wrongly doubles the "l" in the first syllable ("Full-" instead of "Ful-"), which is not a correct spelling in either British or American English.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Fulfilling" is correctly spelt — the present participle form of "fulfil" (doubling the final "l" before adding "-ing", as per the one-syllable-before-suffix doubling rule for a stressed final consonant).

• Option 2: "Fulfil" is correctly spelt — the base form of the verb (British spelling).

• Option 3: "Fulfilled" is correctly spelt — the past tense/past participle form (doubling the final "l" before adding "-ed").

NOTE

• Spelling rule: when a word ends in a single stressed consonant preceded by a single vowel (like "fulfil"), the final consonant is doubled before adding a suffix beginning with a vowel ("-ing", "-ed"): fulfil → fulfilling, fulfilled.

• Other commonly confused doubled-letter words tested by SSC: occurrence, embarrass, harass, accommodate, committee.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Hesitate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Dither.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "hesitate" means to pause or be slow in speaking or acting because one is uncertain or unwilling. (झिझकना / हिचकिचाना)
◦ Example: She hesitated before answering the difficult question.

• Its closest synonym is "dither", which means to be indecisive or hesitate about something. (अनिश्चित होना / हिचकिचाना)
◦ Example: Stop dithering and make a decision.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Haste" (जल्दबाज़ी): means speed or urgency in action — this is nearly opposite to "hesitate".

• Option 2: "Stumble" (लड़खड़ाना): means to trip or momentarily lose one's balance while walking, or to make a mistake while speaking — not the same as hesitating out of uncertainty.

• Option 4: "Hassle" (झंझट): means a situation that is annoying or causes difficulty; used as a noun for "trouble/bother" — unrelated to hesitating.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "hesitate": waver, vacillate, falter, procrastinate (specifically for delaying a decision/action).

• Its antonym is "decide" / "resolve", meaning to be firm and certain in one's action.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
As it is a rainy season, it is raining cats and mice.
option_1: it is raining tigers and lions
option_2: it is raining cats and dogs
option_3: it is raining dogs and wolves
option_4: it is raining birds and beats
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. it is raining cats and dogs.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "raining cats and dogs" means raining very heavily/torrentially. (मूसलाधार बारिश होना)
◦ Example: We couldn't go out yesterday because it was raining cats and dogs.

• The underlined phrase "is raining cats and mice" in the given sentence is an incorrect, distorted version of this well-established idiom; the correct fixed form always uses "cats and dogs", never "cats and mice".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "it is raining tigers and lions" is incorrect — this is not a recognised English idiom.

• Option 3: "it is raining dogs and wolves" is incorrect — again, not the correct fixed idiomatic pairing.

• Option 4: "it is raining birds and beats" is incorrect — this is a meaningless, non-idiomatic combination (and "beats" is not even the correct word "beasts").

NOTE

• Idioms are fixed expressions; substituting even one word (as with "mice" for "dogs" here) makes the expression incorrect, regardless of how similar the meaning seems.

• Other weather-related idioms tested by SSC: "under the weather" (feeling unwell), "a storm in a teacup" (a small matter exaggerated), "come rain or shine" (whatever happens).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
The COVID-19 outbreak has caused a global education crisis.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. catastrophe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "crisis" means a time of intense difficulty, trouble, or danger. (संकट)
◦ Example: The company is facing a severe financial crisis.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "catastrophe", meaning a sudden and widespread disaster or a great and often sudden misfortune. (विपत्ति / महाविनाश)
◦ Example: The flood was a catastrophe for the entire region.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "legacy" (विरासत): something handed down from the past, such as property or a tradition — unrelated to a crisis.

• Option 3: "inhibition" (झिझक/निषेध): a feeling that makes one self-conscious or unable to act naturally; a restraint — not the same as a crisis.

• Option 4: "hoard" (संग्रह करना/जमा करना): to accumulate and store a large quantity of something, often secretly — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "crisis": emergency, calamity, predicament, plight.

• Do not confuse "crisis" (a difficult/dangerous situation) with "criteria" (standards of judgement) — a common SSC vocabulary trap due to similar spelling.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A royal ceremony in which a crown is placed on the head of a new King or a Queen.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Coronation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Coronation" means a royal ceremony in which a crown is placed on the head of a new king or queen, marking their formal investiture with royal power. (राज्याभिषेक)
◦ Example: Thousands gathered to watch the coronation of the new king.

• This one-word substitute exactly matches the given phrase describing the ceremony of crowning a monarch.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Corroboration" (पुष्टि): the action of confirming or giving support to a statement, theory, or finding — unrelated to a royal ceremony.

• Option 2: "Unseating" (पदच्युत करना): the act of removing someone from a position of power or office — nearly the opposite idea of a coronation.

• Option 3: "Ousting" (बेदखल करना): the act of forcing someone out of a position or place — also opposite in meaning to being crowned.

NOTE

• Other royalty-related one-word substitutes tested by SSC: "Abdication" (formally giving up the throne), "Regicide" (the killing of a king), "Interregnum" (a period when a country has no ruler).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Unique
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Exclusive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "unique" means being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else. (अद्वितीय / अनूठा)
◦ Example: Every snowflake has a unique pattern.

• Its closest synonym here is "exclusive", which can mean not shared with others; limited to a single person, group, or thing; one of a kind. (विशिष्ट / अनन्य)
◦ Example: The hotel offers an exclusive suite found nowhere else in the city.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "General" (सामान्य): common, widespread, or applicable to most cases — nearly the opposite of "unique".

• Option 2: "Ordinary" (साधारण): commonplace, not distinctive or special — opposite in meaning to "unique".

• Option 4: "Usual" (सामान्य/प्रचलित): habitually or typically occurring — again, opposite to something one-of-a-kind.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "unique": singular, distinctive, matchless, unparalleled, one-of-a-kind.

• "Unique" is generally considered an absolute adjective (something either is or is not unique), so avoid combining it with "very" or "most" in formal writing — a fact often tested in SSC error-spotting questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom for the underlined segment in the following sentence.
The proud people forget the fact that the world is tangible.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. High and mighty.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "high and mighty" means behaving as if one is more important than other people; arrogant and self-important. (घमंडी / अपने आप को बड़ा समझने वाला)
◦ Example: Ever since his promotion, he has become high and mighty and refuses to talk to his old colleagues.

• The underlined phrase "proud people" in the sentence refers to arrogant, self-important people, which is exactly what the idiom "high and mighty" describes.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Hobson's choice" (जबरदस्ती का विकल्प): a situation offering no real alternative, i.e. "take it or leave it" — unrelated to pride.

• Option 2: "Head and shoulders" (कहीं ज़्यादा बेहतर): used to say someone/something is far superior to others, as in "head and shoulders above the rest" — describes superiority, not arrogance/pride specifically.

• Option 4: "Hard-nosed attitude" (व्यावहारिक/कठोर रवैया): a practical, tough, and uncompromising approach to things — refers to toughness, not pride/arrogance.

NOTE

• Other idioms describing arrogance often asked in SSC: "to be on one's high horse" (to behave in a superior, arrogant manner), "to look down one's nose at someone" (to regard someone as inferior), "to have a big head" (to be conceited).

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in positive degree of comparison.
Istanbul is a beautiful city.
option_1: The city of Istanbul is as beautiful as other cities.
option_2: Istanbul is a very beautiful city.
option_4: No other place I have seen is as beautiful as Istanbul.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No other place I have seen is as beautiful as Istanbul.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Degrees of Comparison (Superlative idea expressed in Positive Degree): To express the highest/superlative quality of a person or thing using the Positive Degree, the standard pattern used is: "No other + noun (+ that I have seen/known) + is as + adjective + as + the subject."

• This construction conveys that nothing else compared is equal to the subject in that quality, which indirectly communicates the idea that the subject possesses that quality to the greatest degree, while still using only the positive form of the adjective ("beautiful"), without "more" or "most".

• Applying the rule to convey that Istanbul's beauty is unmatched: "No other place I have seen is as beautiful as Istanbul."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "The city of Istanbul is as beautiful as other cities" is incorrect — this only states equality with other cities, not that Istanbul stands unmatched in beauty.

• Option 2: "Istanbul is a very beautiful city" is incorrect — this is simply a restatement of the given sentence with an added intensifier ("very"); it does not use the required "No other...as...as" positive-degree construction.

• Option 3: "Beautiful city is the Istanbul" is incorrect — this is grammatically faulty word order and does not form a meaningful sentence.

NOTE

• The three degrees of comparison — Positive, Comparative, and Superlative — can each express the same underlying idea; SSC frequently tests converting between them using fixed patterns like "No other...as...as..." (Positive), "...er/more...than any other..." (Comparative), and "the...est/most..." (Superlative).

• Always keep the same adjective form (positive, i.e. "beautiful", not "more beautiful" or "most beautiful") when converting into the Positive Degree.

question:
Select the meaningful and correctly spelt word from the given options to fill in the blank.
The colourful procession was the last item to be performed in the ___________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. pageantry.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "pageantry", meaning an impressive or elaborate ceremony or display, especially one that forms part of a public celebration.

• In the sentence, "The colourful procession was the last item to be performed in the pageantry" makes complete sense — a colourful procession is a typical part of a grand ceremonial display, i.e. "pageantry".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "peasantry" is a correctly spelt word, but it means the class of peasants/farm workers as a whole, which does not fit the meaning of the sentence about a colourful ceremonial procession.

• Option 2: "pegentry" is an incorrect spelling — there is no such word in English.

• Option 4: "pegeantri" is an incorrect spelling — again, not a real English word.

NOTE

• Spelling key for "pageantry": PAGE + ANT + RY. Related word: "pageant" (a public entertainment or ceremonial display, often with a procession).

• Do not confuse "pageantry" (ceremonial display) with "peasantry" (farming class) — the two look similar but differ completely in meaning, a common SSC distractor pair.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. agenda for sustainable development
B. as the world faces cascading and
C. interlinked global crises and conflicts
D. the aspirations set out in the 2030
E. are in jeopardy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BCDAE.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Reading the parts in the order B-C-D-A-E gives a grammatically complete and logically coherent sentence: "As the world faces cascading and [B] interlinked global crises and conflicts, [C] the aspirations set out in the 2030 [D] agenda for sustainable development [A] are in jeopardy [E]."

• Rule for sentence-rearrangement (Para jumbles): Identify the part that begins with a subordinating conjunction (like "as") to form the introductory/dependent clause, then trace the noun phrase it modifies through to the main clause containing the subject and verb.

• Here, part B ("as the world faces cascading and") begins the dependent clause, which is completed by C ("interlinked global crises and conflicts"); the main clause subject is built up across D ("the aspirations set out in the 2030") and A ("agenda for sustainable development"), which is then completed by the main verb phrase E ("are in jeopardy").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "ABEDC" is incorrect — it separates "the aspirations set out in the 2030" (D) from "agenda for sustainable development" (A), which must stay together as a single noun phrase ("the 2030 agenda for sustainable development").

• Option 2: "CBADE" is incorrect — starting with C ("interlinked global crises and conflicts") without the preceding "as the world faces cascading and" (B) leaves the clause grammatically incomplete and without its conjunction.

• Option 4: "AEDCB" is incorrect — it places "agenda for sustainable development" (A) before "are in jeopardy" (E) too early, breaking the required noun phrase "the 2030 agenda for sustainable development" and disrupting the sentence's logic entirely.

NOTE

• Fixed/compound noun phrases (like "the 2030 agenda for sustainable development") must never be split apart when solving para-jumbles — always look for such fixed phrases first as anchor points.

• Sentences beginning with subordinating conjunctions such as "as", "since", "because" typically state a cause/circumstance before the main clause states its effect/result.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Profit
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Expense.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "profit" means a financial gain, especially the difference between the amount earned and the amount spent. (लाभ)
◦ Example: The company made a huge profit this quarter.

• Its most appropriate antonym among the given options is "expense", meaning the cost incurred or money spent on something, which is the opposite financial concept to a gain/profit. (व्यय / खर्च)
◦ Example: The rising expenses ate into the company's profit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Earnings" (कमाई): money obtained in return for labour or services, or as profit — this is a near-synonym of "profit", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Amount" (राशि): a quantity of something, especially money — a neutral term, not an opposite of profit.

• Option 3: "Sale" (बिक्री): the exchange of goods for money — related to how profit is generated, not its opposite.

NOTE

• The most precise antonym of "profit" in general usage is "loss"; among the given options, "expense" is the closest, since it represents money going out rather than being gained.

• Other common finance-related antonym pairs tested by SSC: income vs. expenditure, credit vs. debit, surplus vs. deficit.

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in active voice.
The meeting was called off.
option_1: The meeting had been called off.
option_4: They were calling off the meeting.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Someone called off the meeting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The meeting was called off" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense, and importantly, no agent ("by...") is mentioned.

• Rule — Converting Passive to Active when no agent is given: When the doer of the action is not mentioned in a passive sentence, the active voice is formed using an indefinite subject such as "someone", "people", "one", or "they" (used impersonally) — with "someone" being the standard, most precise choice for a singular, unspecified doer.

• Applying the rule: "The meeting was called off" (no agent) → "Someone called off the meeting.", keeping the same Simple Past Tense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "The meeting had been called off" is incorrect — this simply restates the sentence in the passive voice (Past Perfect), it is not an active-voice conversion at all.

• Option 2: "They called off the meeting" is incorrect — "they" wrongly implies a specific, already-known group of people, which is not indicated anywhere in the original passive sentence.

• Option 4: "They were calling off the meeting" is incorrect — besides the same "they" problem as Option 2, it also wrongly changes the tense to Past Continuous.

NOTE

• When no agent is given in a passive sentence, always prefer a generic subject like "someone" (for a person, singular action) or "people/they" (for a general, collective agent) over a wrongly assumed specific pronoun.

• Keep the tense of the active sentence identical to that of the given passive sentence unless the rule of voice conversion specifically requires a change.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
I have think tomorrow I will take my belongings to the new apartment.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I think.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined portion "I have think" is grammatically incorrect — "have" (an auxiliary verb used to form the Present Perfect Tense) must be followed by the past participle (V3) of the main verb, not its base form (V1); "have think" is not a valid verb form in English.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense for stating an opinion/belief about a future plan: Verbs like "think", "believe", "hope", "suppose" are commonly used in the Simple Present Tense to introduce a personal opinion, even when the opinion is about a future action (here, "tomorrow I will take my belongings...").

• Applying the rule, "I have think" must simply be corrected to "I think" (Simple Present Tense): "I think tomorrow I will take my belongings to the new apartment."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "I will think" is incorrect — this wrongly puts the verb "think" itself into the future tense, whereas it is the belief being stated now (in the present), about a future action.

• Option 3: "I had think" is incorrect — like the original, "had" (an auxiliary for Past Perfect) must be followed by a past participle (V3, i.e. "thought"), not the base form "think".

• Option 4: "I am think" is incorrect — "am" (an auxiliary for Present Continuous) must be followed by the "-ing" form of the verb (i.e. "thinking"), not the base form "think".

NOTE

• Auxiliary verbs must always combine with the correct verb form: "is/am/are" + V1-ing (continuous), "has/have/had" + V3 (perfect) — mixing these forms is one of the most frequently tested grammar errors in SSC exams.

• Other verbs commonly used in the Simple Present to state a current opinion about future/general matters: believe, suppose, guess, doubt, hope.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

On an unfortunate accident, first aid experts stress that (1)______what to do for an (2)________ victim until a doctor or other trained person gets to the accident scene can (3)________a life, especially in cases of stoppage of breathing, severe bleeding, and shock. People with special problems such as diabetes, epilepsy, or allergy are (4)________ to wear some sort of emblem identifying the problem, as a safeguard against administration of medication that might be injurious or even (5)________.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. knowing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "first aid experts stress that knowing what to do for an injured victim... can save a life." The verb "stress" here means "to emphasise the importance of something", and its object must be a gerund/noun phrase describing the important thing being emphasised.

• "Knowing" (the gerund/-ing form used as a noun, meaning "having knowledge of") correctly fits as the subject of the following clause "...can save a life" — i.e., it is the act of knowing what to do that can save a life.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "regarding" is incorrect — "regarding" is a preposition meaning "concerning/about", and does not fit grammatically as the subject of "can save a life".

• Option 3: "attempting" is incorrect — while grammatically a gerund like "knowing", it does not fit the intended meaning of the passage, which is about being informed/aware, not merely attempting an action.

• Option 4: "before" is incorrect — "before" is a preposition/conjunction of time and cannot function as a gerund-subject in this sentence structure.

NOTE

• When a verb like "stress", "emphasise", or "highlight" is followed by "that", the clause after "that" typically needs a subject that can itself be the doer of a further action — here, a gerund ("knowing") works because it names an action treated as a noun (the subject of "can save a life").

• Gerunds (verb + -ing used as nouns) are frequently tested in SSC cloze passages as the correct fit for a blank that must function as the subject or object of a clause.

On an unfortunate accident, first aid experts stress that (1)______what to do for an (2)________ victim until a doctor or other trained person gets to the accident scene can (3)________a life, especially in cases of stoppage of breathing, severe bleeding, and shock. People with special problems such as diabetes, epilepsy, or allergy are (4)________ to wear some sort of emblem identifying the problem, as a safeguard against administration of medication that might be injurious or even (5)________.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. injured.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage is about first aid for an accident victim, so the missing word must describe the condition of the victim that would require first aid — that is, someone who has been hurt/harmed physically, i.e. "injured".

• The completed sentence reads logically: "...knowing what to do for an injured victim until a doctor or other trained person gets to the accident scene can save a life, especially in cases of stoppage of breathing, severe bleeding, and shock" — all these conditions (breathing stoppage, bleeding, shock) directly describe an injured person.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "efficient" is incorrect — it means capable of working well without wasting resources, which does not describe an accident victim.

• Option 3: "inquiring" is incorrect — it means curious or asking questions, which is irrelevant to describing a victim needing first aid.

• Option 4: "accidental" is incorrect — although related to "accident", it means "happening by chance", and describes an event, not a person's physical condition; it does not fit grammatically or contextually as well as "injured" to describe the "victim".

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check that the chosen word matches both the grammatical category required (here, an adjective describing "victim") and the overall topic/context (first aid for physical injury).

• Related first-aid vocabulary often tested by SSC: casualty, wounded, unconscious, resuscitate, emergency.

On an unfortunate accident, first aid experts stress that (1)______what to do for an (2)________ victim until a doctor or other trained person gets to the accident scene can (3)________a life, especially in cases of stoppage of breathing, severe bleeding, and shock. People with special problems such as diabetes, epilepsy, or allergy are (4)________ to wear some sort of emblem identifying the problem, as a safeguard against administration of medication that might be injurious or even (5)________.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. save.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "knowing what to do for an injured victim until a doctor or other trained person gets to the accident scene can save a life, especially in cases of stoppage of breathing, severe bleeding, and shock." The overall topic of the passage is the importance of first-aid knowledge, and its clear positive purpose is to preserve/save a life in an emergency.

• The phrase "can save a life" is a common fixed collocation used specifically to describe the life-preserving benefit of timely first aid.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "soothe" is incorrect — "soothe" means to calm or comfort someone, which is a much weaker and less contextually complete action than what timely first aid achieves in emergencies like stopped breathing.

• Option 3: "harm" is incorrect — this is the direct opposite of the intended meaning; the whole point of first aid is to prevent harm, not cause it.

• Option 4: "take" is incorrect — "take a life" would mean to kill someone, which is the opposite of the passage's intended positive meaning.

NOTE

• Watch for near-opposite distractors (like "save" vs. "take" a life) in cloze passages — SSC often places a word with an opposite or unrelated meaning as a distractor option.

• The collocation "save a life" is a fixed, frequently used phrase in English related to medical/emergency contexts.

On an unfortunate accident, first aid experts stress that (1)______what to do for an (2)________ victim until a doctor or other trained person gets to the accident scene can (3)________a life, especially in cases of stoppage of breathing, severe bleeding, and shock. People with special problems such as diabetes, epilepsy, or allergy are (4)________ to wear some sort of emblem identifying the problem, as a safeguard against administration of medication that might be injurious or even (5)________.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. urged.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "People with special problems such as diabetes, epilepsy, or allergy are urged to wear some sort of emblem identifying the problem, as a safeguard against administration of medication that might be injurious or even fatal." "Urged" means strongly encouraged or advised to do something, which fits the context of a safety recommendation being given to at-risk people.

• Rule — Passive Voice with "to + infinitive": The structure "Subject + are/is + V3 + to + infinitive" (are urged to wear) is a common passive construction used to express recommendation or advice given to the subject.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "benefitted" is incorrect — "benefitted" does not fit the "are ___ to wear" structure meaningfully; one cannot be "benefitted to wear" something.

• Option 3: "invited" is incorrect — "invited" implies a polite, optional social request, whereas the context calls for a strong safety-related recommendation.

• Option 4: "allowed" is incorrect — "allowed" implies permission is being granted, but the context is about actively encouraging/advising people to take a safety precaution, not merely permitting them to do so.

NOTE

• The passive construction "are/is + past participle + to + infinitive" (e.g. "are urged to", "are advised to", "are asked to") is frequently used in formal/instructional English to give recommendations, and is a common cloze-passage test point.

• Related safety-advice vocabulary: recommended, advised, encouraged, cautioned.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

On an unfortunate accident, first aid experts stress that (1)______what to do for an (2)________ victim until a doctor or other trained person gets to the accident scene can (3)________a life, especially in cases of stoppage of breathing, severe bleeding, and shock. People with special problems such as diabetes, epilepsy, or allergy are (4)________ to wear some sort of emblem identifying the problem, as a safeguard against administration of medication that might be injurious or even (5)________.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. fatal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...as a safeguard against administration of medication that might be injurious or even fatal." The word "fatal" means causing death, and it logically completes the escalation from "injurious" (causing harm) to "fatal" (causing death) — a common rhetorical pattern of listing increasing severity.

• Rule — "or even" construction: The phrase "or even ___" is used to introduce a more extreme/severe possibility than what was just mentioned; since "injurious" (harmful) was already stated, the word after "or even" must denote something worse than merely harmful — i.e., deadly/fatal.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "appropriate" is incorrect — this means suitable/fitting, which does not describe a negative/dangerous outcome of wrong medication and does not fit the "or even ___" escalation pattern.

• Option 2: "beneficial" is incorrect — this means having a helpful/positive effect, which is the opposite of the negative outcome (a safeguard against harmful medication) that the sentence describes.

• Option 4: "remedial" is incorrect — this means intended to correct or improve something, again a positive connotation, which contradicts the negative context of "administration of medication that might be injurious".

NOTE

• The construction **"or even ___"** always signals an escalation to a more extreme, usually more negative/severe, outcome than what was just described — a useful clue in cloze-passage questions.

• Related vocabulary describing severity of harm: injurious < harmful < dangerous < fatal/deadly (fatal being the most severe, meaning "causing death").
